text.content:
This add-on brings OA material from eight issues of Dragon Magazine (#121, 127, 130, 139, 146, 151, 157 and 164) into a 1e FRPG game running the OA Lite module. Everything is restated in plain words with the articles' numbers; you need the magazines for their original text. Like OA Lite, it leaves out the Eastern Lands setting, honor, family, birthrights and castes, and gives prices in standard coins (converted with OA Table 46: 1 fen = 1 cp, 1 yuan = 5 cp, 1 tael = 10 sp, 1 ch'ien = 5 gp).

The Sage Advice columns are clarifications. Everything else (the classes, martial arts, archery, ships, spells for PHB casters, monk orders and police) is an optional supplement: the DM decides what to use. The Hand-to-Hand article in particular is the author's guidance, not errata.

Turning it on

  • Needs the OA Lite module (frpg1e-oa-lite) and 1e FRPG 0.48.0 or later. Switch it on in Manage Modules, then accept the offer to build the OA Dragon compendia. Rebuild them any time from Configure Settings, 1e FRPG: OA Dragon, Rebuild OA Dragon compendia.
  • If OA Lite isn't active, this module stays off and says so.

On the character sheet

  • New classes: Genin (#121), Geisya (#121), Sumotori (Wieck) and Sumotori (Carpenter) (#157), and Piao Shih (#164), with their experience tables, hit dice, attack and saving throw tables. The two sumotori are separate classes, since the magazine printed both and let readers choose.
  • Races: the genin and both sumotori are open to OA humans only; the geisya to OA humans and spirit folk (any level) and hengeyokai (up to 5th); the piao shih to OA humans and spirit folk (any level). (Carpenter's sumotori names no race limit; the module opens it to humans, like Wieck's.) The PHB races give no ruling for these classes.
  • Automatic: the genin's backstab multiplier and attacks per round (as a ninja); the geisya's spells (her own list, "Geisya"); Carpenter's sumotori's armor class by level; Wieck's sumotori's armor class bonuses; the piao shih's +1 to hit and damage with thrown darts and his bushi attacks per round.
  • OA tab: a "Dragon classes" box lists each new class's abilities at its current level, with its proficiency slots.

Things done by hand

  • Genin skills: his thief-like skills are the ninja's (OA Table 24) at his level, shown in the box; roll them by hand.
  • Sumotori hit points: Wieck's sumotori never rolls less than twice his constitution hit point bonus on a hit die, and from 10th level gains twice that bonus each level; Carpenter's gains strength and constitution percentiles by level like the cavalier. Adjust these by hand.
  • Piao shih specialties: the box shows which of his four specialties are open at his level; note his choices and apply them by hand (they improve with the levels gained since each was taken).
  • Weight, initiative and wrestling bonuses for the sumotori, the geisya's arts, and the arrows' armor class adjustments (which replace the bow's) are applied by hand.
  • Experience rules (Carpenter's sumotori earns half experience except by wrestling; Wieck's earns experience by bouts) are the DM's to apply.

What is left out

  • "Earn Those Heirlooms!" (Dragon #151): an inheritance-point system for OA birthrights, built entirely on honor and family. OA Lite has neither.
  • Honor awards and penalties throughout (the geisya's, the police's, the sumotori's, the piao shih's base honor), and Sage Advice answers about honor, birth rank, birthrights, daimyo, the setting's calendar and its currency.
  • The setting's country names in "Soldiers of the Law", and the place names of the authors' own campaigns.

The add-on builds these world compendia.

  • OA Dragon Journals: the articles in plain words, by topic: Using This Module, Sage Advice, Classes, Martial Arts, Archery, Ships, Magic and Treasure, and Monks and the Law.
  • OA Dragon Spells: 108 spells. Geisya (20: her ten own spells and ten OA spells at their geisya level); and OA spells adapted for PHB casters by "Magic from East to West" (#130): Cleric (26), Druid (17), Magic-User (35) and Illusionist (10), each with the article's change at the top and the OA description below it for reference.
  • OA Dragon Martial Arts: 22 styles (the twenty of "A Menagerie of Martial Arts", the sample ninjutsu style, and the sumotori's sumai) and 34 special maneuvers (from "Flying Feet and Lightning Hands" and "Things Your Sensei Never Taught You", plus the sumotori's Strong Slap and Stunning Slap), in folders by category.
  • OA Dragon Proficiencies: the eight genin-only proficiencies, the shobu ceremony (Wieck's sumotori) and paddling (dragon boat races).
  • OA Dragon Equipment: the nine new arrows of "Arrows of the East" (bird, target, six hollow-tip fillings and fishing), each with its armor class adjustments, and the genin's shinobi shozoku.

pages.name: Rulings and the OA Lite Module

text.content:
The Sage Advice answers in Dragon #121 and #151 are clarifications. This module doesn't change OA Lite to match them; the DM decides. These answers differ from how the OA Lite module (v0.1.1) works:

  • Monk attack table (#121): "All monks attack as clerics." OA Lite follows OA's class text and uses the thief table. To follow the ruling, adjust the monk's to-hit by hand.
  • Monks and strength (#121): a monk never gets strength bonuses with weapons or martial arts. The sheet adds strength bonuses to every melee attack, including an OA monk's. Enter an opposite miscellaneous adjustment to follow the ruling.
  • Monk proficiencies (#151): 5 to start, 1 more every 2 levels, nonproficiency penalty -3. OA Lite gives the monk no proficiency row (OA Table 56 has none) and uses the PHB monk penalty, -3. The penalty matches; the slots don't.
  • Yakuza proficiencies (#151): 3 to start, 1 more every 3 levels, penalty -3. OA Lite gives 3 to start and none added. The starting slots and penalty match; the added slots don't.
  • Lajatang (#151): two-handed (its Table 49 entry should be bold). OA Lite marks no weapon as two-handed, since the scan doesn't show the bold reliably.

These agree with OA Lite already: the bushi's first armor class bonus at 5th level; no dexterity adjustment to a monk's armor class; no experience bonus for ninja (#139 and #151 both say OA p.8 is wrong); sohei casting only up to 4th level (OA Lite keeps the 5th-7th level marks with a note that they can't come into play); calligraphy costing two slots.

The two Sage Advice columns disagree with each other on one point: #121 says a grenade is the size and weight of a vial of holy water, #151 a flask of oil.

Based on "Sage Advice" by Skip Williams, Dragon #121 (May 1987), p.20-24 (the OA questions). Rewritten in plain words as questions and answers; adapted for OA Lite. These are clarifications, not new rules. Where an answer differs from how the OA Lite module works, the Rulings and the OA Lite Module page says so.

Characters and combat

  • Height, weight and starting age? Use the DMG tables (DMG p.13-14 and 102). Korobokuru use the dwarf tables, humans and hengeyokai the human tables, and spirit folk the elf tables.
  • Does a dual-classed character get all the proficiency slots of his new class? Yes, all the new class's starting slots.
  • Which classes are open to women? All of them, though some sects may forbid women (or men) as shukenja or sohei.
  • Multi-classed and dual-classed characters? There are no multi-classed OA characters (OA p.28). Humans can become dual-classed under the OA p.28 rules.
  • Experience for money? Yes: 1 xp per 2 tael, which is 1 xp per gold piece in standard coins.
  • Extra attacks at 3/2: the DMG says the second attack comes on odd rounds, OA says even. All characters get their extra attacks on even-numbered rounds. Against an opponent with only one attack (or attack routine), a character with two attacks strikes first and last, as DMG p.63 describes.
  • Crossbow specialists: a crossbow of distance or of accuracy, or an accuracy spell, does not extend a specialist's point-blank range. That range comes from the specialist's skill, not the missile or launcher; the item or spell works normally otherwise.
  • Can PHB and UA characters learn martial arts or OA weapons? Martial arts, yes, if they find a teacher and have a weapon proficiency slot free. OA weapons, if they are like weapons their class allows: a magic-user, for example, could use a slot to learn shuriken, which are like darts. (The article adds that most masters won't teach a foreigner; that is setting detail, left to the DM in OA Lite.)

Barbarians

  • The forest barbarian's rhetoric: according to OA's designer, David Cook, it is the art of long-winded argument: two opponents sit face to face, take deep breaths and talk without stopping, and the first to pause for breath loses. It has nothing to do with logic or elegant words, and it is strictly a barbarian proficiency.
  • The harpoon (a forest barbarian preferred weapon) is described in UA p.26, 27 and 77.

Bushi and kensai

  • When does a bushi get his first armor class bonus? At 5th level, then 10th, and so on.
  • How does a kensai learn martial arts? Can a style be his second weapon? Kensai learn styles like anyone else. A 1st-level kensai who picks a style gets it without spending a slot, and can use his other weapon slot for a special maneuver. A style is an acceptable second weapon. As he gains slots he can add more weapons or maneuvers; the one-extra-weapon limit applies only to his three 1st-level slots.
  • Fast draw with his chosen weapon? A kensai can learn iaijutsu, but if he takes it at 1st level he can't take a second weapon.
  • Psychic duel between two kensai: the higher level doesn't always win. Use the normal procedure; neither gets a bonus against the other.
  • (A question about the bushi's honor loss for ninja weapons is left out of OA Lite.)

Monks

  • Which attack table? All monks attack as clerics.
  • Dexterity and armor class, strength and damage, style armor class? Dexterity never affects a monk's armor class. A monk never gets strength bonuses of any kind with weapons or martial arts. He uses the armor class of his style (its modifier applied to AC 10, or a common style's AC) or of his monk level, whichever is better.
  • Dexterity bonuses to thief abilities? Yes, using OA Table 23 (OA p.19).
  • Does the monk damage bonus apply to missiles and martial arts? The +1 per two levels applies to missile and melee weapons he is proficient with, but not to martial arts; for those, use the Additional Martial Damage column of OA Table 21 (OA p.18).

Ninja

  • Can ninja become dual-classed? No: they are already split class and can't take a third. (But see the genin, a single-class ninja.)
  • Training costs? All OA classes pay training costs (DMG p.86). Ninja pay theirs to their clan.
  • Followers, training younger ninja, gatherings? Up to the head of the clan, played by the DM: there may be gatherings to train or confirm loyalty, and he may tell player ninja to teach clan members.
  • Dexterity bonuses for falling, disguise, escape and tightrope walking? Acrobat abilities? None: for ninja these are a matter of conditioning and discipline, not dexterity. Ninja aren't acrobats and can't use acrobatic maneuvers.
  • Pick pockets? Ninja can't pick pockets. The pick pockets adjustments on OA Table 23 apply only to ninja-yakuza and yakuza.
  • Can a bushi, sohei, wu jen or yakuza become a ninja later, by dual-classing? No. The choice to be a ninja is made at the start of play.

Samurai

  • Specializing: OA p.22 (second paragraph) is misleading. A samurai spends two slots to specialize in the katana and three for the daikyu.
  • (A question about the land and peasants of a samurai's fief or a family's holdings is left out of OA Lite. The answer was that the DM decides, with help from OA p.31-36 and other books.)

Shukenja, sohei and wu jen

  • Full experience for subdued creatures? Shukenja aren't meant to be aggressive except toward evil spirits. They get half experience for other opponents they defeat, by any means.
  • Sohei spells above 4th level: sohei cast up to 4th level only. The sohei marks on 5th-7th level spells in OA Table 62 are errors.
  • Six hours to memorize each wu jen spell? No: six hours in total, however many spells.
  • The wu jen's second ki power: he must already have a spell of the right level memorized; it gives no extra spell.
  • Fire wings: the caster can cast purely verbal spells, but only when landed or gliding.
  • Scry: a flat circle, though common sense extends it upward (floor to ceiling in a room, for example). The DM judges.

Equipment

  • Grenades: use the DMG grenade-like missile charts. Dust and pepper grenades affect one target and need a direct hit. Flash powder and poison smoke grenades must be thrown into a fire to work. Effects are on OA p.50. Grenades are about the size and weight of a vial of holy water.
  • Encumbrance: use the nearest PHB equivalent; rope or clothing weighs the same wherever it is made.

Monsters

  • "Standard" intelligence means average (8-10).
  • Kappa and strength: their damage bonus is already in the listed damage; they do get the to-hit bonus the description gives.

Martial arts

  • Gaining special maneuvers: each maneuver takes one proficiency slot, whatever the style and whatever else the character knows.
  • Two attacks for created styles; karate has three: created styles have at most two attacks. The common styles on OA p.101 weren't made with the creation rules; each is unique and can't be recreated or changed with them. Karate does allow three attacks, and player characters can learn any of the p.101 styles.
  • Weapon styles: learned like any style; the weapon is part of it and needs no extra slot. Only martial arts weapons can be used with a weapon style, and each martial arts weapon needs its own style.

Based on "Sage Advice" by Skip Williams, Dragon #151 (November 1989), p.8-9 and 58. Rewritten in plain words as questions and answers; adapted for OA Lite. These are clarifications, not new rules. Where an answer differs from how the OA Lite module works, the Rulings and the OA Lite Module page says so. (Questions about birth rank, birthrights, honor, daimyo, the setting's calendar and its currency are left out of OA Lite.)

Characters

  • Psionics? Optional, as in any 1eFRPG campaign.
  • Character sheets? The standard character sheets work for OA characters.
  • Calligraphy: the class descriptions suggest one slot, OA Table 61 says two. It costs two slots.
  • Monk and yakuza proficiencies (additions to OA Table 56):
    Additions to OA Table 56 (Dragon #151)
    ClassStarting proficienciesAdded per levelNonproficiency penalty
    Monk51/2-3
    Yakuza31/3-3
  • Gaining levels, training, new wu jen spells: characters gain levels by earning experience and training, and pay training costs (DMG p.86). A wu jen gains new spells when he can cast them and has access to them: at 3rd level he can cast 2nd-level spells if he finds a written copy, learns one from someone, or researches it, and makes his chance to know (OA p.25). The OA p.25 method is the same as the PHB's, so it can be used in any campaign.
  • Researching spells and making items: spells can be researched at any level if they suit the researcher's level (DMG p.115-116). The level needed to make magic items varies (DMG p.116-118); wu jen count as magic-users of the same level for this.
  • Learning languages: anyone can learn a new language if intelligence allows. The DM may let a character forget a language he hasn't used in a long time to make room for a new one; racial and alignment languages can never be forgotten this way. How long it takes is up to the DM; one campaign uses 48 weeks minus the character's intelligence and wisdom.
  • Turns, rounds and segments are the same length as usual (PHB p.31).
  • Peaceful skill rolls: roll the listed number or higher on 1d20. 3 is the lowest adjusted number, so a roll of 1 or 2 always fails. Numbers above 20 come from extra slots spent on the proficiency (OA p.52) or magic items. Ability modifiers don't apply to peaceful skills.
  • Using spells of the other tradition: OA p.130 says 5% of scrolls hold PHB spells, which OA characters can use; in a PHB campaign the DM can reverse this.
  • Gems: use the DMG (p.25-26) for values and properties.

Ninja

  • Experience bonus: OA p.8 says a ninja gets 10% for high dexterity; p.19 says he doesn't. p.19 is correct.
  • Weapons: Table 13 says ninja can use any weapon, but a footnote limits them to ninja preferred weapons. A ninja can learn other weapons with slots from his other class, or with any slot once he knows every ninja weapon.
  • Bushi-ninja strength bonuses, wu jen-ninja spells in armor, ki powers, experience: think of a ninja as a kind of dual-classed character who can draw on either class at any time. Bushi-ninja get strength bonuses. A ninja uses the skills, spells and ki powers of his other class within its limits (a wu jen-ninja can't cast spells in armor). The DM decides when he is acting as a ninja; it only affects experience, and generally experience is split evenly between his classes if he used his ninja abilities during the adventure.
  • Moving silently in armor: metal scale and chain are metal armor. Leather scale isn't, so a ninja can move silently in it.
  • Being found out: a ninja always uses an alias and keeps his real name and family history secret. He should try to hide that he is a ninja, but needn't; it is very hard to hide a character's class in a campaign. (The article's honor penalties are left out of OA Lite.)
  • The ninja-to's secret compartment is very small: one dose of poison, or something the size of a ring or coin.

Samurai

  • Property: a samurai gets the great kiai and followers at 9th level, not property. Earlier he is offered stewardship of properties, not ownership; a 7th-level samurai's stewardship (jito) usually covers one to three villages of his lord's. He needs at least 10th level for the full hierarchy of followers on OA p.22.

Weapons and equipment

  • Two-handed battle axe? No: it was often swung two-handed only because a fighter without a shield had nothing better to do with his other hand. To try two-handed use, improve its speed factor and its adjustment against every armor class by 1, and make its damage 3-9 (2d4+1); weight, length and space required are unchanged.
  • The lajatang is two-handed: its Table 49 entry should be bold.
  • Needles (said to be used for assassinations): treat as chopsticks.
  • Weight of OA equipment: use the nearest regular or real-world equivalent; rope or clothing weighs the same wherever it is made. Grenades are about the size and weight of a flask of oil. (Dragon #121 said a vial of holy water.)
  • The table at the bottom of OA p.50 is Table 55, just above the text.
  • Two-weapon fighting: the usual rules (DMG p.70). Any OA weapon equivalent to a dagger or hand axe can be the second weapon (OA Table 48). A kensai's second weapon must be a dagger or hand axe or an equivalent, so no pair of katanas. Extra slots can't remove the two-weapon penalty; only kensai of 7th level or more fight with two weapons without it.
  • Iaijutsu gives no initiative modifier: the character can draw or change weapons with no penalty, and in some cases has a better chance to surprise (OA p.99).

Martial arts

  • How many styles? In theory as many as he has weapon proficiencies, but it would be a waste; weapons or special maneuvers are better uses of slots.
  • Learning maneuvers in order: a style's maneuvers are learned in numerical order whatever their group, using only the maneuvers in the style. In tae kwon do, Movement 5 is learned last; the character doesn't learn (and can't) Movements 1-4, which aren't in his style.
  • Which maneuvers suit a created style: the style's form decides. Each maneuver in OA Table 70 is labeled hard, hard/soft or soft: hard maneuvers go mainly with hard styles, soft with soft, and hard/soft with any. Mental and physical training maneuvers are labeled with their best forms but can go with any style. Other maneuvers should stay in their form; a good rule of thumb is no more than one out-of-form maneuver per style.
  • To-hit rolls for maneuvers: Sage Advice in Dragon #122 said Leap rolls against AC 10. That doesn't extend to other maneuvers: combat maneuvers generally roll against the target's armor class. In Weapon Catch, the target is the one holding the weapon.

Monsters and adventures

  • Generals of the animal kings: their frequency doesn't apply; they appear only when their kings send them on errands, where and when the DM decides. On a special encounter table they should be very rare at best.
  • A dungeon encounter table? Make your own. The OA monsters and the notes in the second monster book (p.138) will get you started.
  • The badger hengeyokai (OA p.13) is the raccoon dog on OA Table 11.

Based on "The Genin: A single-class ninja for OA campaigns" by David Howery, Dragon #121 (May 1987), p.42-43. Rewritten in plain words; adapted for OA Lite.

In OA the ninja is always a split class: every ninja also lives as a bushi, sohei, wu jen or yakuza. Historically, ninja came in three ranks: the jonin, who headed the ninja clans; the chunin, the go-betweens and messengers, who are most like OA's split-class ninja; and the genin, the operatives who carried out most missions. Genin sometimes led a double life, but more often they lived only as ninja, in remote camps in the mountains. The genin is a ninja who is nothing else: either his double life is as an ordinary person with no class (a merchant, a minor official and so on), or he has no double life at all.

Requirements

  • Same ability scores and alignment as the ninja: dexterity 14, charisma 14 and intelligence 15 or more, and any non-good alignment.
  • No prime requisite, so no experience bonus.
  • Humans only.
  • (The article also gives the genin the ninja's honor and family requirements; OA Lite has none.)

Experience and combat

Use the Genin Experience table below in place of the ninja's (OA Table 22). Genin roll six-sided hit dice, attack on the thief table and save as thieves.

300,000 experience points for each level beyond 12th. +1 hit point per level beyond 10th.

Abilities

A genin has all the abilities of a ninja of the same level: the skills on OA Table 24 (hide in shadows, move silently, climb walls, disguise and the rest), the ninja's ki powers, the ninja's multiple attacks (OA Table 36) and the ninja dexterity adjustments (OA Table 23). Trained from childhood, he also has these extra abilities:

  • Hear noise as a monk of the same level. He can also learn things from what he hears: how big a door or gate that opened is, how many people are in a room, whether a sleeper is faking.
  • Disguise as a ninja, but he can get out of a disguise quickly, in one full round.
  • Maps: an excellent sense of direction and memory for landmarks let him read maps and draw accurate ones.

Proficiencies

A genin starts with five proficiency slots. Two must go to the ninja-to and the bo stick; the other three can be non-weapon proficiencies, martial arts or other weapons he may use. He gains one slot every three levels after 1st (at 4th, 7th, 10th and so on). He can learn any artisan, common or court proficiency; most learn horsemanship, dance, animal handling and small water craft first. These proficiencies are open only to genin:

  • Binding: ties a person so that he can't move or struggle without great pain.
  • Leaping: the same as the martial arts special maneuver Leap (Movement 5, OA p.103-104).
  • Poison: prepares poisons that kill by smell, taste or touch, and knows how to handle and apply them to best effect.
  • Running: by controlling his breath he can run 50 miles without stopping; walking 15 minutes of every hour, 100 miles.
  • Side-walking: moving his feet sideways at one quarter his normal speed halves the chance to track him.
  • Signaling: sends short, simple messages with flags, gestures or objects left behind.
  • Survival: like the barbarian proficiency, but he can provide only for himself.
  • Swimming: as the common proficiency, but he swims silently, and can swim upright to hold things out of the water, write or even use a bow.

Money, clothing, weapons and tools

A 1st-level genin starts with 5 or 10 gp (1d2 × 5 gp) and 20-200 sp (2d10 × 10 sp). (The article gives 1-2 ch'ien and 2-20 tael; converted with OA Table 46.) He wears no armor except as a disguise. His usual adventuring clothes are the shinobi shozoku: a light suit of jacket, hood, trousers and tabi boots, reddish black and reversible, with a dark blue lining and enough pockets for all his usual gear. It costs 6 sp (12 yuan).

A ninja can use any weapon, but a genin is limited to these lists:

  • Ninja weapons: grenade, hankyu, kawanaga, kumade, kusari-gama, kyoketsu-shogi, metsubishi, needle, nekode, ninja-to, shaken, shuriken (all) and tetsu-bishi.
  • Genin weapons: arrow (all), blowpipe and dart, bo stick, chain, halberd, kama, kiseru, shakujo-yari, shikomi-zue and spear.
  • Martial arts weapons: any, if he has the proficiency in a martial arts weapon style.

Ninja and genin often carry these (the DM can add more):

  • Climbing tools: nekode or te-kagi (clawed grips for smooth stone, +5% to climb walls); musubinawa (short, strong horsehair rope); shinobi kumade (telescoping bamboo rod with a grapnel hook at one end).
  • Infiltration tools: lock pick, chisel, wood or metal saw, digging knife, springboard; tobi-kunai (a tool for digging, prying, boring, cutting and wedging); tsuba-giri (a heavy fork for springing doors).
  • Water devices: folding straw rafts, small portable boats, snorkel, rope and pulley; mizugumo (foot pontoons for walking upright on water).
  • Weapons used as tools: a bo stick can pole vault up to 8 feet; the hole in a star shuriken pulls nails; the ninja-to scabbard serves as a snorkel, club or lever, holds powder or small knives in its bottom, and its long cord makes a garrote; a sheathed ninja-to leaned against a wall makes a 2-foot step, standing on the large handguard.

Other notes

  • A genin who isn't leading a double life spends all his time between adventures training at his clan's base camp.
  • Men and women alike become ninja of both kinds.
  • A genin will die rather than be captured, since captors often torture prisoners for information. He may carry poison for this, and may even bite through his tongue to silence his cries.
  • (The article's honor penalty when a clan's base camp is found is left out of OA Lite.)

Based on "The Geisya: An OA class with subtle skills" by Gregg Sharp, Dragon #121 (May 1987), p.38-41. Rewritten in plain words; adapted for OA Lite.

The geisya is an artist and entertainer, much like the bard: she sings, dances, plays music and makes up poetry on the spot, and she has some minor magic and parlor tricks. (Gei means art and sha means person.) She is not a prostitute; that is the yujo or korobi geisha, not covered here. The article presents the geisya as a non-player character class, usable by players only if the DM allows it.

Requirements

  • Intelligence 12, wisdom 12, charisma 11 and dexterity 13 or more. No prime requisite, so no experience bonus.
  • Lawful alignment.
  • Humans and spirit folk have no level limit; hengeyokai can reach 5th level. No other race can be a geisya.
  • Geisya are almost all women. The rare man is an otoko geisya, a comic or jester.

Experience, combat and equipment

+1 hit point per level beyond 6th. The article says 250,000 experience points are needed "for every level beyond the 7th", though the table runs to 9th; the module uses 250,000 per level after 9th. Levels 6 and 7 are printed overlapping at 20,101; kept as printed (7th begins at 20,101).

  • Four-sided hit dice. She attacks and saves as a magic-user.
  • Starting money: 5-30 gp (1d6 × 5 gp; the article gives 1-6 ch'ien, converted with OA Table 46).
  • No armor, shields, oil or poison. Weapons: naginata, dagger, knife, gunsen, kiseru and shuriken. Using a weapon she isn't proficient with is -6 to hit.
  • A geisya-ninja (split class) uses oil, poison and any weapon she likes, and often needles.
  • Geisya never gain special attack bonuses or abilities. Some of their spells are defensive.

Proficiencies and specialization

  • Four proficiency slots at 1st level, only one of which can be a weapon (usually the naginata, since a geisya helps defend the castle where she is engaged). She must take etiquette at 1st level. The rest can be any proficiency except barbarian ones. She gains one slot every level.
  • At 2nd level she picks one art to specialize in: her primary skill, never a weapon skill. Specialization takes two proficiency slots and at least six hours of practice a week to keep. The maiko (1st-level apprentice) plans her training toward it.
  • By 5th level she must have the dance, music and poetry proficiencies.
  • At 4th level she can meditate as a shukenja.
  • Every two levels she can learn another language if she finds a teacher, up to half her intelligence. These are often old court languages, and may include the geisya cant: finger and fan gestures for silently passing simple messages to another geisya.

A geisya is not a fighter. She gets out of trouble by other means: flattery has won over oni and soothed tengu, and great artistic skill is prized by almost all monsters, so a skilled koto or shamisen player may calm some of the cleverer ones. (Bakemono are tone-deaf and simply hungry.)

Specialized arts

A geisya who has mastered, or nearly mastered, one of these arts gains its extra ability:

  • Brewer: makes many liquors, especially sake, and can distill pure grain alcohol to burn, or for others to use as a weapon against siege engines.
  • Masseuse: eases muscle cramps by massage, and can strike pressure points: a hit and a successful proficiency roll give the victim -2 to hit for 1-4 rounds.
  • Dance: great endurance and speed: +2 to her base movement rate, and she doesn't tire easily.
  • Juggling: keeps a number of daggers in the air equal to 13 minus the number she needs on the proficiency roll (needing 8, she juggles five). It takes a round to get two daggers in the air, and she can throw them all at a target in the same round.
  • Music: one instrument (shamisen, koto or another) and its musical forms. Besides the base chance that her music soothes the semi-savage, a specialist can try a charm person with a successful proficiency roll. It works only on some creatures, though some animals are calmed by music; saving throws and magic resistance apply. Only a calming, unthreatening message can be sent; she can give no spoken instructions.
  • Singing: a specialist whose singing roll is down to 12 can use legend lore at 5% per level for relics, artifacts, people, places and events of myth and legend.
  • Etiquette: flatters without it showing. A successful roll raises one person's reaction roll by 10%; a failure lowers it by 10%.
  • Flower arranging: offerings left at shrines are judged by priests and spirits. A fine one may bring good luck (+1 to saving throws for a day); a poor one, bad luck (-1 for a day). The DM decides.
  • Poetry: the impromptu poet is also a riddle master, and may get an extra clue in the riddle game.

Special abilities

  • Prestidigitation: picks pockets as a ninja two levels lower.
  • Disguise: as a ninja one level lower.
  • Feel spiritual presence: 5% per two levels to detect unseen or hidden spirits. (Many geisya retire to temples, and gentler spirits seek them out for their art.)
  • Game play: she can steer a game such as go so that her opponent barely wins. She has 5% per level to know the details of a given game; if she knows it, there is a 25% chance she plays it at expert level. An expert's chance to win is 7% per level.

A geisya casts spells from her own list. Most are entertainments; a few protect her.

Sumo wrestling

Two wrestlers (sumotori) meet in a ring (dohyo) 15 feet across, under a roof made to look like a shrine, with spectators in matted boxes on every side, often with tea or sake at hand. Each may grab any part of his opponent's upper body or his mawashi, the stiff silk loincloth that is his only clothing. A bout (shobu) is won by forcing the opponent out of the ring or making him touch the ground with anything but the soles of his feet. It looks simple, but every hold and throw is defined; 48 classic throws are recorded. Most bouts last under 10 seconds; a few run to five minutes, though bouts not settled in the first minute or two are usually stopped and restarted. Wrestlers can't protest: the judges' decision is final, though a bout too close to call can be fought again.

  • Forbidden: punching with a closed fist, hitting below the belt, bending back fingers, clapping both ears at once, pulling hair, breaking bones, gouging eyes and choking.
  • Allowed: punching with the heel of the hand, butting, grabbing the upper body, tripping, slapping, straight-arming, pushing against the jaw and grabbing the mawashi.
  • Each bout has two wrestlers, a referee and up to five judges (fewer at smaller tournaments, basho). Two large tournaments a year is suggested for a campaign.

Sumotori are almost always over 6 feet tall; the lightest weigh over 200 lbs, and many twice that. They gain their size by devoting themselves to the sport young, eating a stew of cabbage, carrots, onions and bean curd with soy sauce, sugar and fish (chanko-nabe) twice a day with huge amounts of rice; apprentices cook for the elder wrestlers. In the end a champion wins less by size than by awareness: out-thinking the opponent and catching him in a moment of relaxation.

The sumotori class

  • A subclass of bushi. Attacks and saves on the fighter tables. Twelve-sided hit dice; a hit die roll is never less than twice his constitution hit point bonus (with constitution 17, bonus 3, he gets at least 6).
  • Lawful male humans only. Minimum strength 16, dexterity 12, constitution 14 and wisdom 13. No experience bonus for high abilities.
  • No armor, shields, weapons, oil or poison: he fights only with hands and body. He avoids magic items in the ring, where they are strictly forbidden. He gains no henchmen or hirelings.
  • Four proficiency slots; at 1st level one must be the shobu ceremony (one slot, base number 13; without it he can't take part in any bout) and one cooking. He gains a slot every four levels. As he rises he learns the sumo style automatically, without spending slots.
  • Few dare an evil act in the ring, which risks the bout.
  • Experience: from bouts: winning earns 10 times the opponent's hit points, losing earns his hit points. A player sumotori can earn experience the usual ways, but his limits make that hard.
  • The article suggests sumotori be non-player characters, since wrestling is everything to them. If a player wants one, the DM should impose training like the kensai's (OA p.17), and might allow magic rings or bracers that help armor class and saving throws; he still uses no weapons or armor.
  • Training: physical and spiritual. Most good sumotori come from or train in the high mountains; they wade deep snow to build their hips and pound their arms on wooden poles (teppo) to harden the skin. Spiritually, sumo is governed by the Shinto religion: ritual and moral standards matter, though most sumotori simply believe the gods (kami) live in all things in nature.

The shobu ceremony

Before each bout, required of every sumotori; failing it may shame him. He rinses his mouth with water and throws salt into the ring (purifying himself and the ring), enters, squats and claps loudly (calling the gods' attention), slowly stretches his arms toward his opponent and turns his palms to show he holds no weapon, and stamps to drive off evil spirits that might affect the bout. Then he tries to unsettle his opponent, glaring belligerently or not deigning to glance at him, and moves about slapping his body to prepare.

Running a bout

  1. Each wrestler makes his shobu ceremony roll. A failure loses the +3 psychic duel bonus. (The article adds possible honor loss; OA Lite has no honor.)
  2. The psychic duel (OA p.100-101). The winner gets +2 to his Sumo Number.
  3. Each wrestler's Sumo Number is the total of: Iron Fist +2, Locking Block +2, Immovability +3, Hurl +2, Great Throw +4, Ironskin +1 (for those he knows); +1 per four points of strength (each step above 18 counts as one point); and +2 for the psychic duel winner.
  4. Both roll 1d20 and must roll his Sumo Number or less to avoid losing. If both fail, they make no real contact for 1d10 seconds and roll again. A wrestler wins if he passes while his opponent fails, or, if both pass, by rolling higher. Each pair of rolls takes twice the difference between the rolls, in seconds.
  5. If both pass with the same roll, the higher Sumo Number wins, and that roll took 20+1d20 seconds. If the Sumo Numbers are equal too, it took 50 seconds plus the time of further rolls, which continue until there is no tie or a minute has passed.
  6. A bout longer than a minute is restarted: any winning rolls are ignored, and new ceremony and psychic duel rolls are made.

Example: Shiro (3rd level, strength 15) faces Kanka (6th level, strength 18/30). Both spend their daily ki on strength. Shiro: Iron Fist 2 + Locking Block 2 + strength 17 (4) = 8. Kanka: 2 + 2 + Immovability 3 + Hurl 2 + strength 19 (6) = 14. Only Shiro makes his ceremony roll (Kanka forgot to rinse his mouth), so Kanka loses his +3 in the duel; Kanka loses the duel and Shiro's number becomes 10. Both roll 19, over their numbers: 11 seconds pass (rolled on 1d20). Next Kanka rolls 13 and Shiro 1: the difference of 12 adds 24 seconds, and Kanka wins. At a large tournament a wrestler may have several bouts a day, so he can't use his ki for strength every time.

The sumotori is a non-player character class, rarely an adventurer: very powerful in one narrow field, wrestling, and limited in everything else. He earns his living wrestling at noble courts or public shows. A court wrestler, fed and trained at great cost, is a status symbol for a samurai lord, like a champion racehorse, and a famous one brings fame to his lord as well as himself. Some travel from town to town challenging local champions in open-air bouts, a hard life for a man with such an appetite. An out-of-work sumotori may hire out as muscle for a yakuza band or minor official: bouncer, bodyguard, debt collector or enforcer. The author offers him for color (a warlord's bodyguard, a yakuza enforcer, an imperial court wrestler, an ally or hired muscle for a special mission), not as another class for players.

The sumotori class

  • A subclass of bushi, but a poor warrior: he attacks on the cleric table and saves on the fighter table. Ten-sided hit dice; highest level 8th. Otherwise treated as a fighter subclass, using the magic items fighters can, within his weapon and armor limits.
  • Lawful (good, neutral or evil). Minimum strength 16, constitution 16, intelligence 11 and dexterity 11. No prime requisite and no experience bonus.
  • No armor or shields, no oil or poison. He can be proficient with only one weapon, ever, of any kind except ninja weapons and martial arts weapons that need long study; the mace, club, hammer, maul and tetsubo are typical. Nonproficiency penalty -3.
  • Growing stronger: like the UA cavalier, he has a percentile score after his strength and constitution. At each new level he rolls 2d10 and adds it; when it reaches 100 or more, the ability rises by one. He does this at every level up to 8th.
  • Experience: full experience for winning a wrestling bout or wrestling combat, and for prizes or treasure won by wrestling. Experience earned any other way is halved (wrestling an ogre down earns full experience; clubbing it to death with a tetsubo, half).
  • School: at 8th level he can open a sumo school, attracting 10d4 zero-level students, who each need 5-8 months of hard training to become 1st-level sumotori. A school usually needs an important patron: a powerful lord, a rich yakuza or a social-climbing merchant.
  • Martial arts: his martial arts improve with level, somewhat like a monk's, but he studies only the art of sumai: no other style, no other maneuvers mixed in, and no new styles.

The sumo match

Sumai is an old, no-holds-barred art (said to date from a match in 22 BC) whose aim is to kill with deadly locks and blows; from the 8th century the most dangerous holds were banned and the stylized sport of sumo grew from it. Women wrestlers were rare but not unknown in feudal Japan. The match takes place in a circular ring 15 feet across; a wrestler loses if he touches the ground with anything but his feet or is forced out. The aim is not to hurt but to prove superiority of mind and body in a disciplined bout. Bouts are fast and often over in seconds, so the key is initiative each round, and winning the opening psychic duel is crucial.

  1. Each wrestler performs the traditional ceremony of ritual moves and gestures, an art in itself, to win the gods' favor and entertain true enthusiasts.
  2. They face off in formal stances and try to intimidate each other: a psychic duel (OA p.100-101). The loser doesn't give up, but is -1 to initiative, saving throws and to-hit rolls.
  3. In a civilized match only Stunning Slap, Hurl, Immovability and Immobilizing are allowed; normal martial arts attacks and Strong Slap aren't used, since they take too many blows to fell a foe.
  4. Novices without those maneuvers use simple overbearing or grappling. The defender resists overbearing with his strength bonus as armor class, or with Immovability. After a grappling hold, the attacker's next attack can move the defender to the edge and try to push, pull or lift him out: a hit roll, resisted the same way. He can keep trying until the defender is out or breaks free.
  5. Higher-level wrestlers use the maneuvers: Stunning Slap to stun before grappling or overbearing; Hurl, the most common attack, since it gets round the defender's strength bonus; Immovability to stay put; and an Immobilizing lock used like a grappling hold but at +4 to force the defender out.

Example: Kurudo (7th level, AC 6, 64 hp, to-hit 14 with strength, 2d6+2, 470 lbs: distance -5, Immovability/stun save 6) faces Yori (6th level, AC 7, 51 hp, 440 lbs: distance -4, save 8). Yori wins the psychic duel, 17 to 8, so Kurudo is -1. Yori wins initiative and Hurls, hitting with 14 (needing 11), but Kurudo makes his Immovability save. Kurudo traps Yori in an Immobilizing lock (19-1=18), and could force him toward the edge at +4, but Yori pushes his strength to 18/00 and breaks the hold (15 +3 -6 = 12; breaking an Immobilizing lock is at -6). Kurudo's Hurl misses (5-1=4), so he loses initiative next round (OA p.104). Yori's Stunning Slap hits (16); Kurudo fails his save by one (6-1=5) because of the duel penalty, and Yori pushes the stunned Kurudo out of the ring. Based on "Born to Defend: The piao shih, a guardian character for OA games" by Joseph R. Ravitts, Dragon #164 (December 1990), p.26-31. Rewritten in plain words; adapted for OA Lite (honor, birth rank and the setting's name left out; money converted to standard coins with OA Table 46).

In real-world China, from ancient times through the 19th century, merchants and officials crossing vast distances hired professional caravan guards, martial artists to match any Shaolin priest. Such a guard was a piao shih, literally "dart master", since they were experts at throwing heavy darts at bandits; many Chinese adventure films are about them. In a game the piao shih livens up journeys with a new kind of character met along the road, reminds everyone how big and hard to police the land is, and gives visiting PHB characters a hireling or ally who can guide the uninitiated.

The class

  • A mix of bushi and monk, with a dash of ranger. Humans and spirit folk only, with no level limit.
  • No ability score below 12; at least 15 in strength or dexterity, and at least 15 in wisdom or charisma. No experience bonus.
  • Usually lawful neutral, but any lawful or good alignment. Lawful evil piao shih exist only under an evil government. Never chaotic, except chaotic good: a habit of betraying or abusing clients would ruin a piao shih's reputation and business and stop his advancement.
  • Eight-sided hit dice. Any armor or shield, though most wear leather, studded leather or padded. Fighter attack and saving throw tables, with as many attacks a round as a bushi.
  • Four proficiency slots, one more every two levels; nonproficiency penalty -2. Peaceful proficiencies from the artisan, barbarian, common and court lists.
  • Magic items usable by all classes and by fighters, and any magic weapons or armor. Oil in combat; only lawful evil piao shih use poison.
  • Starting money: 5-20 gp (1d4 × 5 gp) and 10-100 sp (1d10 × 10 sp); the article gives 1-4 ch'ien and 1-10 tael (ch'ao).
  • Henchmen and hirelings allowed, and followers come with level (below).

If he ever founds his own organization, this first pupil may come along as second in command (though taking many people from the parent group would be disgraceful). He now has more authority over the party he guards: equal to the highest social class in it, for decisions about the journey.
  • 9th: when he takes charge of any caravan, he has complete control over its servants who aren't piao shih (a nobleman's longtime bushi bodyguard, say, or the monk teaching martial arts to the nobleman's son). Usually he also gains a permanent troop: two lieutenants of 4th-6th level and 10-12 piao shih of 1st or 2nd level.
  • 10th: may command a force of three or more piao shih troops (even from different, friendly organizations) to guard major caravans miles long. Once a day he senses approaching danger as with the psionic talent precognition (PHB p.113): unconsciously, when normal means such as scouting fail, and only in wilderness he travels regularly.
  • 11th, Master of Escorts (the level table calls 11th "Captain of Escorts" and 12th "Master of Escorts"; as printed): may found his own escort business, if he finds open territory, or lead his present organization if its leadership is vacant. The new organization attracts 4-16 zero-level men-at-arms of compatible alignment; half can become piao shih, the rest guard its headquarters. He should design a banner at once, usually with a slogan such as "Our darts bring lightning from the clouds" or "All serpents are crushed beneath our horses' hooves".
  • 15th, banner: if he reaches 15th level without a humiliating defeat (the DM judges), his banner commands deep respect. Hostile beings (short of outer planes beings) who see and recognize it, borne by anyone who looks able to defend himself, must check morale before coming within 100 yards. Members of his organization or of friendly piao shih groups get +10% morale when they see it in friendly hands. Anyone in a psychic duel with him who can see it counts as two levels lower.
  • 17th: he carries at least as much weight as a minor nobleman in the government's decisions on travel and trade; in effect he enters the nobility.

Specialties

Over his career a piao shih picks four specialties: two tactical and two strategic, at the levels on the table (a piao shih with dexterity 18 gets each tactical specialty a level sooner; with wisdom 18, each strategic one). A specialty improves with the levels gained since he took it, not with his total level: a 3rd-level piao shih who takes Ground Fighting and another who takes it at 7th use it at the same skill.

Tactical specialties

  • Base Defense: for defending a fixed place: any building more complex than a small tent or bare hut, and at the DM's option some outdoor places such as a graveyard or an elaborate palace garden. He studies the place beforehand, the way a blind person learns his home: where the furniture is, how far across a room, how wide the doorways. Fighting there, he gets +2 to armor class and saving throws against any attack that solid barriers can hinder (diving behind furniture, ducking round corners), and +1 to hit (yanking rugs from under foes, slamming doors in their faces). In total darkness these bonuses double, unless the attackers can see in it; at the DM's option he also has -2 on any roll to hit his own allies by mistake in the dark.
    • At first he must spend at least 24 hours in a place (more for large ones, such as a whole castle) to learn it, and can know only one place at a time. One level after taking it, the time is halved; two levels after, 1-4 hours is enough; three levels after, he can keep two places in mind (usually one is his headquarters); four levels after, with intelligence 16 or more, one more place per point of intelligence over 16 (a string of refuges along his route, though bandits may burn them while he is away).
    • With Trap Construction too, in the same place: thieves, assassins and hostile monks fighting him there have -35 to detect the traps he has set, since he maneuvers them into setting them off, and each time he succeeds he gets an extra melee attack on that enemy at +1.
  • Combat Horsemanship: every piao shih rides and fights from horseback; with this he gets +1 to any horse's speed without tiring it more. One level later, he can keep a mount from panicking at any ordinary cause of fear (it saves at +2 against magical fear); two levels later, +1 to armor class fighting from horseback (hanging along the horse's side and other evasive moves); three levels later, +2. (The DM can add this to dexterity bonuses to armor class, but not to monk missile dodging rolls.)
  • Ground Fighting: fights well crouching, prone or low (in caves, on ice, at night on cluttered ground): +1 to armor class there against foes without the skill. He never takes more than half damage from being tossed or thrown down, and has 5% per level since taking it to escape all trampling damage (in a stampede, for example). Two levels later, +1 to armor class against the first attack of any flying creature diving from above, unless he is completely surprised.
  • Scaling: he already climbs as a monk; with this he can get others up. With climbing gear to lend, he gets one client up at his own chance of success; one level later, two clients; three levels later, one client even with no special gear. With constitution 14 or more and time spent at high altitude, he functions normally where others faint from thin air.
  • Water Skill: swims half again as fast and holds his breath half again as long as he otherwise could, and handles any small boat of his home region. One level later, he fights on a wildly pitching deck without losing his footing; two levels later, if he falls into water in armor or other load that would drown him, he can get free of it in time (unless unconscious); three levels later, he can do every task of crewing a large seagoing ship (and with intelligence 14 or more, navigate); four levels later, he swims or paddles in perfect silence, improving the chance to surprise.
  • Weapon Mastery: superior skill with one weapon besides darts, taught by a senior piao shih who has mastered it or a kensai who uses it. No to-hit bonus, but +1 to armor class against opponents using that kind of weapon, and 1% per level since taking it (up to 10%) to kill any man-sized or smaller foe instantly with a hit (never giant-class beings). The weapon is defined narrowly for the kill chance and more broadly for the defense: a daikyu master, drawing with the thumb, gets no kill chance with an unfamiliar long bow, but his armor class bonus applies against all arrows. With a blunt weapon he can make the kill a nonlethal subdual instead. A piao shih with dexterity 16 or more can take Weapon Mastery as both tactical specialties, with two weapons.

Strategic specialties

  • Crowd Control: keeps order among the caravan's non-piao shih: preventing quarrels, accidents and panic in dangers other than bandit or monster attacks, and keeping a retreat from overwhelming odds from becoming a rout. It works on members whose level is no higher than his: as many as his charisma, plus two per level since taking it. Useful when members want to explore somewhere he knows is dangerous, or food must be rationed. It isn't magic: those he protects keep their free will, and player characters who obey him voluntarily are added to his total. Two or more piao shih with it add their numbers, as long as their orders don't conflict. (The article's honor exemption is left out of OA Lite.)
  • Environment Augury: like the druid spell predict weather, but also predicting earthquakes and avalanches: 30%, +5% per level since taking it.
  • Graphology: martial artists (other than priests) were never highly regarded socially and seldom educated, so every piao shih below Master is illiterate, unless he has intelligence 16 or more or some stroke of luck (saving a scribe's life and being taught as a reward, say). A literate piao shih can take Graphology: he understands unfamiliar written languages at 1% per point of intelligence, +2% per level since taking it, and spots forgeries of any handwriting he sees often (a merchant's, an official's). One level later, 5% (+5% per level) to detect invisible ink and other hidden writing. Four levels later, he can create a small private set of marks and symbols to teach colleagues for secret messages.
  • Pass Without Trace: like the druid spell: 90% on foot, 60% mounted on a horse or similar animal, if he isn't being watched when he starts. On a success normal beings can't follow his trail; rangers and other trackers treat it as the next worst terrain. He can cover others' tracks too: each person on foot with him (without the skill) subtracts 2%, each horse or similar animal 6%, and wagons or very large animals make it hopeless unless the ground makes it easy (open fields under snow, say). Four levels later, he can spend a movement turn laying a false trail: +5% per level from then on to hide the party's true direction, and +10% at any level if a caravan animal is sent running along the false trail. Magical tracking still defeats all this.
  • Poison Warding: needs an alchemist or someone else who knows poisons to teach him. 6% per level since taking it to detect poison in food, drink, on weapons and so on (3% per level for sophisticated split poisons, such as one part in the wine and another in the meat). From the start he can make preventive medicines that cure 2 hit points of poison damage, +2 per level since taking it; each works against one particular poison only (a scorpion sting remedy is useless against snake venom or poisonous mushrooms).
  • Recruitment: in recruiting trainees and persuading merchants, officials and others to hire his organization, his charisma counts as 3 higher, even above 18. (Using it to defraud people may bring revenge from the victims and from scandalized piao shih.) Piao shih trained by someone two or more levels past taking this specialty get +10% experience all their careers, as long as their specialties don't differ greatly from their trainer's. When he founds his own organization, 8-32 recruits come, plus any compatible piao shih whose own captains have been killed.
  • Sensitivity to Scrutiny: only with wisdom 15 or more and some contact with beings that gather information by psionic or magical means. +20% to detect magical scrying (DMG p.141); a piao shih's base chance is 4%, so 24% on taking it, plus bonuses for intelligence and level.
  • Trap Construction: sets traps around a camp, at the doors of rooms his party uses at an inn, and on chests and other containers. He develops his own repertoire (snares, pits, poisoned needles, fixed crossbows and so on); some traps become an organization's signature. He knows as many kinds as his intelligence above 10, plus one per level since taking it (not counting the simple covered pit anyone can make). Only an evil piao shih uses poison or acid in traps. Four levels later, his traps are harder to disarm: a thief has -5% per level from then on.

Rules and restrictions

The class looks powerful and complicated, but the complexity falls mostly on the DM, and like the paladin it has balancing restrictions.

  • Experience: mainly for delivering people, goods and treasure safely, worked out as the experience others would get for killing or capturing the people and taking the goods (as the DM adjusts). If the team faced no danger at all, only a quarter of that. Killing or capturing enemies earns experience only when it is directly part of the job; otherwise half. For every person in their care who dies, is lost or is kidnapped, every piao shih above 1st level in the party loses experience equal to that person's experience value, and the leader twice that. This never costs a level, but can delay the next one. Losing very valuable client property counts the same way, unless it was given up to save the clients themselves. (Only non-good piao shih value cargo above lives.)
  • Conduct: piao shih rely on spotting others' tricks, not on secrecy and stealth. They identify with the established order and work openly. They may not lie or deceive, except for the safety of fellow piao shih, clients, or their own loved ones, in that order (non-good organizations make no allowance for loved ones). Being drunk on duty, mistreating clients or disobeying a superior piao shih can get one expelled. One who willingly helps bandits or joins them faces death with the worst tortures available, and gains no more experience.
  • Negotiating safe passage with bandits and monsters isn't treachery, unless he secretly takes kickbacks that cost clients too much. A piao shih (whose world is the open road) may sometimes trade information and favors with yakuza (whose world is the city). Piao shih don't try to rid the world of criminals; they protect their charges by practical means. Under strong provocation they strike back: if a robber chief a Master always dealt with in good faith hires assassins against him, the Master can rally his own and every friendly organization to destroy that chief.
  • Territory: such cooperation depends on organizations respecting each other. A new escort organization may not work a trade route another already handles without its consent; the piao shih themselves, local governments, merchants' organizations and even thieves' guilds (fearing trouble from newcomers) enforce this. A formal duel between escort captains may settle a dispute. A leader who takes another's route by treachery faces the same penalty as one who turns bandit, and (unless he is evil displacing a good one) his own followers may desert him in disgust.

Based on "A Menagerie of Martial Arts: Twenty martial arts styles based on man, nature, and animal" by Len Carpenter, Dragon #127 (November 1987), p.48-55. Rewritten in plain words. An optional supplement: the DM decides which styles and rule changes to use.

OA gives only four real-world styles. This article adds twenty for the campaign: twelve ancient styles named for animals, studied by most classes (though monks are most of their students), and eight newer styles made for the needs or philosophy of a particular group. They are the author's own campaign styles, not simulations of real martial arts. Each is in the OA Dragon Martial Arts compendium.

Some styles change official maneuvers; these are marked below. The DM can drop any change he doesn't like, or replace it with an official maneuver.

Suggested rule change: the naginata

The author strongly recommends adding the naginata to the weapons that can perform the weapon style maneuvers (OA p.42, footnote f). The naginata is a close relative of the spear, wielded in similar ways for similar roles, and the two are often taught side by side. The nagimaki, which falls between the spear and the naginata, can also perform weapon style maneuvers, though it is much less popular.

How the animal styles arose

Ancient ascetics spent years, even decades, in the wild watching an animal until they mastered its every attack, defense and move. The early monks studied mammals, birds, insects, reptiles and even rare magical beasts, and very different systems could come from the same animal: one tiger school might stress the cat's stealth and leaps, another its claws and bite. Rival teachers argued and feuded; eventually the styles gathered into great schools, whose students named themselves for their animal. New styles grew from them, some mixing older animals' attacks and maneuvers, others built around new weapons such as the nunchaku, tonfa (tui-fa) or sai, and some made for particular groups: ninja, women of the court, holy pilgrims.

The twelve animal styles

  • Bear: a wrestling art. The bear strikes hard, crushes with locks, can't be moved if it doesn't want to be, and thinks only of attack. Students master all locks and holds, crushing or stunning blows, and resisting being moved or thrown. No weapons are taught; students use their class's weapons and like heavy ones that need great strength, such as the tetsubo or two-handed sword. Popular with bushi and yakuza.
  • Cat: based on small, quick cats (civet, lynx, even the house cat): speed, active defense and deft footwork rather than crushing power. Students attack fast and by surprise with a flurry of blows, defend by footwork and feints, survive great falls and spring up at once, train with a partner to follow and counter any move, and learn to move and fight in the dark; their awareness lets them kick a foe behind them with a twist of the body. They favor twin daggers, like claws. Popular with women, who also train with the naginata. Some ninja study it to add Blind Fighting to their own styles.
  • Cobra: choose the moment with care, strike a vital point with precision and power, then lock on with an unbreakable grip: pure offense, trusting to win before the foe strikes back. Students study anatomy for vital points; the cobra's jaws inspire its locks. The final goal is Distance Death, striking at range as the cobra spits. No weapons favored. A favorite of ninja and very aggressive warriors.
  • Crane: the crane strikes with beak, legs and wings, withdraws to study a foe and returns to strike; it avoids or deflects an attack, then answers with a swift cut to a vital point. Students use foot and fist equally, dodge and deflect missiles with superb footwork, and keep a strong, alert mind. Schools teach different weapon pairs, used two-handed: two jo sticks, two nunchaku, two sai, sword and jitte, sword and war fan (gunsen), or sai and chain, and stranger pairs in some schools.
  • Dragon: powerful kicks (the sweeping tail), overpowering fist blows (the claws), an immobilizing lock (the jaws), and iron-hard skin (the scales). Students favor high-damage weapons such as the naginata or halberd. Every dragon school teaches the kau sin ke, like the sweep of the tail; some also teach the chain. Popular with all kinds of warriors.
  • Dragonfly: perhaps the rarest and most mysterious style. Students try to be as light and quick as the insect, with total control of motion and energy; they let their ki merge with an opponent's and then direct his motion wherever they like, deflecting any attack or sending a foe reeling with the gentlest touch. They learn Flowing Water (their Mental 5; see the note above). The ultimate secret, taught only to the most worthy, is levitation. Weapons are almost always ignored. Rarely studied except by monks and shukenja.
  • Hawk: swift attack and unfailing aim: powerful fist blows, choking locks, accurate finger strikes to nerve centers, and a flying kick like the hawk's dive. Students usually scorn weapons. Favored by those who think offense matters far more than defense.
  • Leopard: speed, cunning and awareness: silent stalking, deceptive moves, and a sudden burst of attack. Students train grace, rhythm and feints, pounce with great leaps and flying kicks, and copy the leopard's trick of holding prey to rake it with its hind claws: a Locking Block followed by sharp kicks. The final goal is Speed (Movement 6). They prefer clawlike weapons such as the dagger, short sword or kama. Popular with those who want speed and power together.
  • Mantis: the small mantis beats much bigger insects by skill. Students use a hooked hand to strike and lock arms, and copy its hops with many kicks and great leaps; fluid footwork is the key to its defense. Weapons are sometimes taught, by class or the teacher's taste.
  • Monkey: an agile, acrobatic trickster who lures foes into mistakes and uses everything around him: trees to escape, vines to swing into position, sticks to strike from a distance. Students master rolls and falls, strong throws and crushing locks, fight from a low crouch and even from the ground, and learn the bo and jo sticks (sometimes the tonfa, kiseru or tetsubo), though a cunning mind is always the best weapon. A variant, the horse-monkey, based on the great apes, learns Strike 3 (Eagle Claw) instead of Movement 2 (Prone Fighting) and has a base AC 7 instead of 6.
  • Snake: lessons from many snakes, biting and constricting: control of every fiber of the body, swift strikes, twisting away and curling back to strike again. So complete is the student's control that he can't be held or hindered, and at last can't be magically slowed. Students strike vital points, capture foes with a choking hold, fight in any position including prone, and rise as fast as a snake strikes. Weapons vary by school and region. Sought by those who want an evasive defense with a solid offense.
  • Tiger: overwhelm the foe with crushing blows and kicks before he can strike back; a choking lock (the jaws) and a flying kick (the pounce). Students often use great slashing weapons such as the naginata or halberd, though many scorn weapons, since the style lacks nothing in power.

The eight specialized styles

  • Bone Breaker: one of two styles taught only within ninja clans: the power of the tiger and cobra with the speed and awareness of the cat. Hard fist blows, nerve strikes, disabling a limb with a sudden attack, smashing an opponent's weapon with his own, fighting blind at night, and Ironskin (from ninja ki training rather than the dragon). He always learns Weapon Breaker with two weapons taught in the clan; popular ones are the sai, jitte, spear (shakujo yari), bo stick and chain. Teaching it to an outsider carries a mandatory death sentence.
  • Dark Hand: another secret ninja style, like Bone Breaker but leaning on the cobra's attacks and the cat's defensive speed. Students learn weapons to catch or shatter an opponent's weapons, including all martial arts weapons ninja favor. Teaching it to an outsider means certain death.
  • Eight-Legged Man: the mantis's footwork and kicks with the speed of the cat styles: fast, precise footwork to get in as many kicks as possible, spinning like a top to kick in every direction (some variants are likened to the spider or octopus). The student needs strong, supple legs, must get up instantly when knocked down, and stays aware of everything around him. No weapons. Aggressive and demanding; unpopular with gentle pilgrims and those unwilling to practice constantly.
  • Eye of the Hurricane: from the dragonfly, with techniques from the monkey and cat styles. The student unites body and mind in calm perfection, learning patience, clear thought and understanding of others; amid chaos he stays calm. Defensive speed and control of the opponent come first: attacks are turned aside harmlessly and the foe subdued rather than hurt, and mystic ki roots him to the ground against any attempt to move him. He can push himself to bursts of offensive speed, but his aim is always defense. He learns Flowing Water (see the note above). No weapons. Popular with monks, shukenja, some wu jen and other spiritual martial artists.
  • Fist within Glove: for pilgrims, monks, nuns and other peaceful folk who need protection without obvious arms: restraint and discipline, violence only as a last resort, aggressors subdued with as little harm as possible. The student avoids or even flees a fight, but can defend himself and others with a pilgrim's staff or bare hands. He trains with unobtrusive weapons that look like tools or traveler's gear: bo stick, jo sticks, kiseru, tonfa and the like. Another common weapon is a hardwood flute 2-3 feet long, used as a jo stick, that whistles a swirling tune as it swings. Some monks and shukenja are said to carry magical flutes that turn their ki into spell-like songs, like a bard's instrument, each with its own set of songs.
  • Oaken Grip: the kicks and footwork of the dragon and mantis with powerful hardwood weapons: solid footwork for defense, flamboyant kicks for offense, and a body trained to resist injury. He uses the three-piece rod, nunchaku or tonfa to strike, catch a weapon, grab an arm or disable a limb. With one of these weapons he can perform Locking Block or Incapacitator; without one, a lock is -2 to hit, since he trained to lock with a weapon. No other weapon can make an oaken lock.
  • Silken Spear: taught to women of the court, from empress to handmaiden, who are expected to fight in need for themselves or their clan with weapons, everyday things and their surroundings. She masters the spear and naginata together for the weapon style maneuvers, and Arrow Cutting (knocking missiles aside with the spear or naginata, not the hands). She can also use the steel cloth spear (Weapon 3) for the other weapon maneuvers and for arrow cutting; without a spear, naginata or steel cloth spear she can still try to deflect missiles at -4 on her saving throw. Unarmed she would rather improvise: a stool or bench serves as a tonfa with speed factor 6-8. Some carry hidden weapons: a dart or dagger in the sleeve, a fan with steel ribs (a gunsen), small razors under long fingernails, perhaps poisoned (a nekode with speed factor 1, for damage), or a kanzashi, a sharp ornamental hairpin often holding deadly poison (a nekode doing 1-3 damage to small or man-sized foes, 1-2 to large ones). Female ninja (kunoichi) often learn it to pass as a handmaiden or lady's bodyguard, with an arsenal hidden in their clothing.
  • Sword Breaker: made by town police to deal with unruly swordsmen; constables and town defenders of the bushi or yakuza class learn it against drunken samurai and other lawbreakers. Strong wrestling with catching and breaking a samurai's blades, usually with the sai or jitte (most constables learn the jitte; elite officers carry the sai as a mark of rank). Poorer towns favor weapons made from farm tools: bo stick, jo sticks, tonfa or chain. The sode garami is popular for entangling and subduing a criminal. Sohei and palace guards sometimes learn a version of it to disarm and subdue without wounding, since spilling blood in a palace or temple is sacrilege in some lands.

Designing new styles

Make each new style special but keep its power within reason. Link maneuvers into a logical, imaginative style around one strong idea: an interesting animal, a colorful phrase, a martial arts book or a flashy movie stunt. Give a maneuver an unusual twist, find new uses for martial arts weapons, and see what new combinations come out of OA Table 69. Try radical ideas outside the campaign first; inside it, keep unusual styles for non-player characters until you are sure they suit players. Err on the side of caution: martial arts help the game only when they are fair and balanced, not when they produce unstoppable killing machines.

Based on "Hand-to-Hand Against the Rules: Modifying the martial arts of OA" by Vince Garcia, Dragon #139 (November 1988), p.58-61 and 64. Rewritten in plain words. Guidance for the DM, not binding errata.

OA's martial arts rules leave gray areas: the kensai can specialize in an unarmed style, but his class table assumes a melee weapon; it isn't clear whether a bushi can specialize in a style; and nothing says a martial artist needs a minimum dexterity (though it is hard to picture a dexterity 3 character landing a circle kick). A dexterity minimum of 10 or 12 seems reasonable, but it would clash with the shukenja, who has martial arts from 1st level and can have dexterity 3. These are the author's suggestions, class by class.

Who can learn martial arts?

Learning Martial Arts (OA p.105) suggests anyone with a free proficiency slot can learn if he finds a master. Only the monk and shukenja have martial arts by right, from 1st level. For the rest, the DM decides, keeping game balance and how well martial arts fit the class in mind.

  • Barbarian: his class is built on skills from a harsh upbringing, and martial arts aren't among them; he would have little reason to take on such demanding, foreign training. Nothing stops him, but the DM decides whether it comes at the expense of his other talents.
  • Bushi: styles are weapon proficiencies, so a bushi could specialize in one, but the specialization benefits make no sense for unarmed styles. The bushi must study under a master and must declare his specialty when created. As an option, a bushi specializing in a style can start with a master if he first goes through a zero-level apprenticeship (like the UA cavalier), working off the experience and hit point penalties on the table below while learning his style from a relative or acquaintance:
    • At zero level he has three proficiency slots, two of which go to the basics of his style. At 1st level he gets the fourth, for a special maneuver or martial arts weapon taught in the style.
    • If he then or later becomes proficient with a martial arts weapon, he gets +1 to hit and damage with that one weapon (not later weapons, nor weapons not used in martial arts).
    • He also gains the bonuses on the Martial-Arts Specialist table: extra martial attacks and damage, a special maneuver of his style every six levels (besides any he buys with slots), and a mental and physical training maneuver of the DM's choice every seven levels.
    • The DM should think hard before letting a bushi who specialized in a weapon learn martial arts later: weapon specialization means constant practice, and so does a style, and an adventuring bushi may not have time for both.
  • Kensai who chooses an unarmed style: his class doesn't require a teacher to start with martial arts, so he needn't go through zero level, though the player and DM may like it anyway (his special maneuvers need supervised training); his table is below.
    • At zero or 1st level he gets the basics of his style free, plus three proficiency slots, one of which can go to martial arts if he has a master. (Not for the style's martial arts weapons, which he can teach himself.) From 2nd level he can spend up to two slots a level on martial arts. Other slots can go to peaceful proficiencies, but until he has mastered every maneuver and weapon of his style, he should learn no other weapons or styles.
    • His bonuses are on the Alternate Bonuses for Kensai table, which moves some kensai abilities to different levels. "A" gives +1 to hit and damage with one martial arts weapon of his style, cumulative and stackable on one weapon if he likes. "G" gives a free proficiency in a martial arts weapon of his style (lost if he already knows them all).

Finding a master

OA p.105 says "master" is an honorary title, not a measure of skill or level. Taken literally, a player kensai could teach a player wu jen jujutsu, which takes this part of the game out of the DM's hands and makes the search for a master pointless. The author suggests player characters learn martial arts only from non-player characters, never from each other. Monasteries guard their styles: a bushi asking a shukenja to teach him tae kwon do should get a polite, firm refusal, and even two adventurers from the same monastery need a temple superior's approval. A ninja never teaches ninjutsu to outsiders, a yakuza never reveals his band's techniques to those outside his oyabun's authority, no one else could endure a kensai's training, and a samurai may think it beneath him to learn from a mere bushi. Often the teacher will be the character's own superiors; for monks, ninja, samurai, shukenja, sohei and yakuza this is nearly certain. Others may have to find a master well away from their friends and superiors.

Once a master is found, the DM uses the OA rules to decide what he knows. For monks, shukenja, sohei, ninja and yakuza, even a limited master isn't a dead end: a more skilled one should not be hard to find later through the same process.

Introducing them

Bring new maneuvers in gradually, especially the advanced ones. Some can be added to existing styles; others can build new styles; some may be secret techniques that masters are slow to teach player characters (sumotori won't readily teach the Crushing Hug to anyone else). Think carefully before letting player characters have them: some suit non-player martial artists best, and a character's first meeting with a new maneuver should often be at the hands (or feet) of an enemy. Thauberger warns that his Slash and Blunt maneuvers are very powerful; the DM may limit them or not allow them at all.
