Fleshing out a style

Thauberger's advice for making created styles more than shopping lists of maneuvers: give each a life of its own, fitting the society and history it came from. A few notes are enough.

  • Appearance: picture the feeling it gives rather than exact moves. Showy or ruthlessly efficient? Fast and reckless, or slow and deliberate? Admired for beauty and simplicity, or thought ugly and crude? A style's popularity varies by region and era; old-fashioned in one province, revered for tradition in another.
  • Social background: peasants have little time for martial arts, so peasant styles are simple and practical with few maneuvers; noble or court styles are more complex and artistic, valued for beauty as much as use. Classes have their own styles too: yakuza and ninja surely have secret ones, wu jen or samurai may favor certain styles, and geisha, archers, actors or carpenters might each develop one.
  • Availability: background limits access. Commoners have trouble finding teachers of noble styles, and nobles resist peasant styles. Availability also varies with place and fashion: some styles have several masters in every province, some only one or two hard-to-find masters, and a few may be only legends.
  • Mental discipline: attach a common, artisan or (for a noble style) court proficiency that needs discipline and skill with the hands, such as weaving, pottery, dance or origami. It can be a prerequisite, or taught free as part of the training; either way it makes martial arts-minded players take some practical skills too.
  • Special maneuvers: add your own to make styles unique, with care. A good maneuver is no stronger than a good 1st- or 2nd-level spell; saving throws should be plentiful, and very powerful maneuvers should have awkward (not too severe) results when they fail.
  • Name: tie it to the style's look or background. OA suggests animals; mythical beasts, forces of nature (wind, rain, lightning) or even clothing (a "kimono" style) also work.

Three examples:

  • Tin Hat: rough, simple and practical; developed by peasant farmers, popular with bushi; very common everywhere; mental discipline: cooking (preparation, patience).
  • Pen and Ink: graceful, precise and beautiful; a nobleman's style; uncommon among the nobility, very rare among the lower classes; mental discipline: calligraphy (style, appearance).
  • Howling Monkey: outrageous and humorous; developed by traveling entertainers; rare everywhere; mental discipline: juggling (coordination, quickness).

The examples give background only; their maneuvers and weapons are left to the DM. Other Dragon articles on creating styles: "Marshalling the Martial Arts" (#122), "A Menagerie of Martial Arts" (#127) and "New Kicks in Martial Arts" (#136).

Based on "The Eastern Sea: The high seas of the OA world" by Margaret Foy, Dragon #130 (February 1988), p.65-69. Rewritten in plain words; prices converted to standard coins with OA Table 46. An optional supplement.

The article brings historical Chinese ships into OA campaigns, using the ship rules of "High Seas" in Dragon #116 (p.10-27). Its tables are numbered to fit with that article's (Table Id follows #116's Table Ia, and so on). You need #116 for the rules these build on: sailing speed, maneuverability and direction (its Tables Ia, Ib and III), damage (its Table VI) and fire (its Table VIII). Defensive points are a ship's hit points (DMG p.54-55 and 109-110). The author drew on G.R.G. Worcester, The Junks and Sampans of the Yangtze (Naval Institute Press, 1971).

Whatever people do on land, they can do on water: floating inns, shops, teahouses, even duck farms. A great river system can carry thousands of miles of navigable water; the real Yangtze, with its tributaries and canals, has 5,500 miles serving 750,000 square miles, and boats drawing 5 feet in winter and 14 feet in summer reach 1,000 miles inland.

How the ships move

  • Sail: the typical sail is a square lugsail with battens. It hangs from a lug (a kind of yard) slung from the mast two thirds of the way along; its head is shorter than its foot (usually three fifths as long), and its foot is laced to a boom. Battens are bamboo strips sewn across the sail and tied to the mast: they keep it flat so the ship can sail closer to the wind, make reefing and lowering easy (the sail folds like a fan), keep it drawing wind even when full of holes, and serve as ladders for climbing the sail.
  • Hull: junks and sampans have flat, keelless bottoms, a square bow and a high stern. They were the first ships with bulkheads (walls across the hold), making watertight compartments that also strengthen the hull.
  • Oars: the rower stands facing forward and pushes the oar, usually one rower per oar. Rowing and sailing are often combined for speed.
  • Sculling: a long sweep, the yuloh, hangs over the stern and is worked side to side like a fish's tail. It can be so long that the sculler stands on a high platform amidships; its weight is balanced so it is easy to work.
  • Poling: pushing a pole against the river bed, walking it from bow to stern. It works only in water 10 feet deep or less.
  • Tracking: hauling the boat with ropes from the shore, the hardest way to move it and the only way up rapids. The heavier cargo is unloaded and most of the crew go ashore. Each tracker wears a harness tied to a bamboo rope; the track may cross creeks, canals and boulders, or be cut into the side of a gorge.

Rapids

Rapids form where a river bed drops suddenly, where the river is partly blocked, or where it enters a gorge; dangers include boulders, rocks, whirlpools, boils and backwaters. Many rivers become shallow stretches broken by rapids when the water falls in winter; others turn to torrents in summer. Before tracking a boat, settle five things: how long the rapids are, how many trackers are needed, how long it takes, what it costs, and the chance of getting through without disaster.

  • A very hard stretch: a mile long, nine hours, 200 trackers paid 5 cp each (one yuan) for 5 gp in all (10 tael), with a 65% chance of success.
  • A very easy stretch (or a canal gate): 10 yards, half an hour, 12 trackers paid 1 cp each (one fen) for 12 cp, with a 95% chance.
  • Roll percentile dice to track or shoot the rapids. On a failure the vessel takes damage as Table V (rapids). When its hull reaches 0 or less it breaks up and everyone aboard goes into the water: each saves versus paralyzation every 20 yards of rapids or takes 1-6 damage.

Crews

A junk's crew is often one family, sometimes with three generations of captains in turn. The captain is the laodah ("old great"). The t'ai-kung is the bow lookout, who works the bow sweep (if there is one) and takes soundings with a long boathook. The shao-huo-ti is the cook, who also buys provisions. The hsien-ch'ueh ("man of all work") is the ordinary sailor; the pa-liang-chia-ti ("one who has to climb") is the able seaman.

OA's shukenja and wu jen lists borrow many PHB and UA spells. This article goes the other way: it adapts OA spells for the four PHB spell-casting classes (cleric, druid, magic-user and illusionist), choosing spells that don't depend on an Eastern setting and leaving out those that overlap PHB and UA spells too closely. A few spells are reworked into new ones. Material components, levels, casting times and effects often change; each change is in the spell's entry in the OA Dragon Spells compendium (folders Cleric, Druid, Magic-User and Illusionist), at the top of the OA description.

Bring the spells in a few at a time: on scrolls, in hard-to-find spell books, or granted by deities as clerics and druids prove themselves. The most fun is when player characters are the first targets of a spell nobody has seen (a fighter caught by magnetism, a thief made lawful good by compel). The DM can drop any spell that doesn't suit the campaign, or add others from OA.

Cleric spells

All come from the shukenja list. Spirits and kami have no PHB counterparts, so the shukenja spells that deal with them aren't given. Clerics don't know the Eastern shapechangers, so detect shapechanger and force shapechange become two new spells about lycanthropes instead. Most PHB races rarely reincarnate, so clerics rarely use remember's second use. Shukenja are always good, while clerics serve a particular deity and can be any alignment, so remorse is unsuitable (forbidden to clerics), and oath, instruct and compel are widened so a cleric of any alignment can use them. Clerics care less about the future than shukenja, so omen and fate come at higher levels.

Based on "The Deadliest Perfume: The properties of lotus blossoms and dust in OA" by John P. Brown, Dragon #121 (May 1987), p.26-30. Rewritten in plain words; adapted for OA Lite.

The article is written as the notes of an old court scribe who gathered ancient lore about six kinds of lotus, and rumors of two more (the gray and the blue). Lotus flowers are dangerous, very rare treasures. If any still grow, they will be in hot, swampy places: tropical swamps, marshes and coastal jungles. The DM places them where he likes, keeping them extremely rare. Ninja clans, sages and the like may know where some grow, but that knowledge is costly and may not be for sale at all.

The flower and its scent

  • Lotus grow in thick, leafy bushes carrying from one blossom (the black lotus) to a dozen (the green). Each flower grows on a stalk up to 3 feet long.
  • The scent is an aphrodisiac (brown, red and yellow lotus) or a strong sedative (black, green and purple lotus). The gray lotus's scent is said to cause catalepsy, and the blue's pleasant hallucinations.
  • Anyone within 10 feet of the plant who fails a saving throw versus poison at +1 is affected for as long as he stays there. After he leaves, the effects fade over 10-60 turns. A damp cloth over nose and mouth protects against the scent.
  • Aphrodisiac: the victim falls in love with the first person of the opposite sex he or she sees, who becomes irresistible to the victim, for as long as the scent reaches him. This is like a philter of love, except that neutralize poison, not dispel magic, cures it. There is a 10% chance it lasts 2-5 weeks. The victim will grant any reasonable request of the loved one if he fails a 1d20 roll against the loved one's charisma, but never does anything that puts himself in danger; if the loved one is in danger, he may give every aid he can. Two characters can be affected at once without necessarily loving each other (though they might). (The article's extra save for requests that cost honor is left out of OA Lite.)
  • Sedative: the victim's speed and dexterity are halved while he is within smelling range. In 5% of cases the effect lingers for 1-4 weeks after he leaves.

Harvesting and preparing the dust

A picked flower starts to decay after two days, so the dust must be made within that time:

  1. Wash the flower in water from a hot spring.
  2. Put it in a bowl of pure silver (any other metal ruins it) and leave it uncovered in total darkness for a day; it turns to paste.
  3. Spread the paste around the inside of the bowl and bake it in a moderate oven (about 100°F) for two days. The resulting dust is the color of the petals.
  4. Store it in an airtight glass vial. One flower makes one dose; a full dose is needed for the effects below.

The usual way to use the dust is to throw the vial at an opponent (sometimes blowing it from a blowgun). It breaks into a hemispherical cloud 10 feet across that hangs in the air for 1-4 minutes, depending on wind and on spells that move air. Purple lotus dust doesn't work this way; it must be eaten or drunk.

Lotus are hard to find and harvest: beasts that prefer to eat people love their scent. Reptiles enjoy the scent but aren't affected, so snakes and biting lizards are a special danger, and dragons are said to be immune too.

The dusts

  • Black lotus (dull black orchid-like flower, shinier black center and pistils; the rarest): the victim falls unconscious at once and must save versus poison at -2 or die in 1-4 minutes. The article's text says no antidote, magical or holy, can help a doomed victim, while its rules note gives neutralize poison 5% per level of the caster to help; both as printed. A survivor sleeps 1-6 hours, then suffers -2 on attacks and saving throws for 2-12 hours more.
  • Brown lotus (light brown petals, dark brown center, gray pistils; quite rare): the victim must save versus poison or suffer the equivalent of a feeblemind for 2-5 weeks. A successful save still costs 1-4 points of intelligence, each regained after an hour's rest. Neutralize poison removes the effects at once. Recovery needs quiet rest; each day of hard mental work delays it by a week.
  • Green lotus (deep green petals, light green center, bright yellow pistils; the most common): paralysis for 7-12 hours if a saving throw versus poison at -1 fails, or 4 hours or less if it succeeds.
  • Purple lotus (red-violet petals, deep purple-black center, bright yellow pistils): must be swallowed. In 1-12 hours the victim falls sick for 1-4 days, with his hit points cut by 90% (round up), which only magical cures such as neutralize poison restore. At the end he must save versus poison at -2 or die.
  • Red lotus (like the purple, with reddish-orange petals): a failed save versus poison brings 5-8 hours of bizarre, terrifying hallucinations of every sense, run by the DM. At the end, a second save versus poison at +2 is needed to avoid random permanent insanity.
  • Yellow lotus (wide yellow petals, yellow pistils, glossy brown center): a failed save versus poison halves strength and dexterity (round up) for 3-6 weeks. A successful save still costs one point of each for 2-8 turns. Recovery needs rest and freedom from moving; each day of hard physical activity delays it by a week.

Any potion, spell or magic item that cures poisoning removes the effects of any lotus scent or dust except the black lotus. Neutralize poison, a scroll of protection from poison and similar magic protect against both scent and dust. Otherwise victims heal at the normal rate.

Rumored lotus

  • Gray lotus: probably imaginary, and linked in every account to necromancy and the negative material plane. Its scent is said to cause a trance while the victim is near it, fading 1-4 hours after he leaves; a save versus poison at -2 avoids it, and a failed save has a 5% chance of a trance lasting 5-30 days. In the trance the victim is paralyzed and mentally fogged, as if stunned. Necromancers are said to use the dust (made with some unknown extra ingredient, perhaps the bones of undead) to make mindless servants: a victim who fails a save versus poison obeys the first person to command him, and no one else, for 2-9 days, though not if told to harm himself (as charm person). The DM decides the details if it exists in the campaign.
  • Blue lotus (sky-blue orchid-like flower, dark purple center, deep blue-black pistils; the most powerful): its scent causes mild, pleasant hallucinations. Breathing the dust (if the DM allows it): on a failed save versus poison (automatic if the user wants it to work) the user's spirit seems to leave his body for 2-20 rounds and he can look into nearby places, as the psionic disciplines clairaudience and clairvoyance together, while his body lies limp. Afterward he feels sleepy and tired for a while. Used more often than once every five days, it calls for a system shock roll, or he dies 1-4 rounds after breathing it. Mixed with at least 5,000 gp of diamond dust, it doubles the range and duration of any divination spell (no other spells), for no longer than a day.

OA put the monk in his proper setting, but left open what monks are for: why the PHB calls them "monastic ascetics", and whether their temples have any purpose beyond being martial artists' hangouts. Every good example of monkish orders in fiction has a mission, a reason for being. The DM should create orders for his campaign, rather than having monks just quote poetry and kick the tails of those who exploit the weak.

Examples from fiction and the game

  • The Zinja (Robert Shea's Shike novels, War of the Dragons and Last of the Zinja): an ancient Japanese brotherhood whose secret mission is to turn the new samurai class into civilized soldiers rather than bloodthirsty killers. Day to day they pass as the finest bodyguards and mercenaries around.
  • The Bloodguard (Stephen R. Donaldson's Thomas Covenant chronicles): fierce mountain tribesmen who came to conquer, but swore a vow to serve the gentle Lords and the Land, as bodyguards and messengers.
  • The Scarlet Brotherhood (the Greyhawk setting): a ring of assassins and thieves ruled by an order of evil monks seeking to make the Suel people the master race (see the module WG8, Fate of Istus).
  • The White Mountain School of the Warrior Saint (Will Shetterly's Witchblood): formed when cruel witches ruled and denied people weapons, so the followers learned to make anything a weapon, even hands and feet. They overthrew the witches but, tired of bloodshed, let them live, and still train and watch in case the witches rise again.
  • The Shaolin of the Kung Fu television series: besides perfecting themselves in body and spirit, they teach and help the local people.

Creating an order

  1. Mission: the most important step: what are the monks trying to do? One line often suffices. A secondary purpose usually follows, often the means to the first (working as bodyguards to defend a nation's rightful rulers). Monks cultivate art and beauty in their training and see their mission as divine and demanding perfection, which is why they withdraw from society to train for it.
  2. Skills and equipment the mission needs: healing or calligraphy for the Shaolin, running or survival for the Bloodguard.
  3. Training: related to the skills but worth thinking about separately. The Shaolin give initiates menial work to teach humility; the Scarlet Brotherhood makes recruits compete for monk training; the Bloodguard learn fighting in their tribes' wars; the Zinja are trained from the start not to fear death.
  4. Alignment: usually clear once the mission is set; monks must be one of the three lawful alignments (the Shaolin are surely lawful good, the Scarlet Brotherhood lawful evil).
  5. Martial arts style: gentle protectors who subdue, or vicious fighters who end things fast and for good? (See Things Your Sensei Never Taught You, in the Martial Arts journal, for building styles.)
  6. History: who founded the order, and why: one man's dream, or a group who saw something that had to be done. Has it made allies or deadly enemies of other sects? Does it have a symbol (the Shaolin's branded forearms, the Zinja's willow tree)?
  7. Reasons to adventure: why would a monk leave his temple? Kwai Chang Caine flees after killing a prince; the Zinja hire out as mercenaries and bodyguards; the Scarlet Brotherhood's members are spread across the world on its business.

Three sample orders

  • The Order of Enlightened Seekers (lawful good). Founded after a war destroyed great numbers of artworks and writings, to stop such a loss happening again. Its monks travel far and wide collecting histories, art, music, records of customs and other writings, and store them in a great stronghold whose location only the Masters of the Order know, safe for future artists and historians. Their temples, marked by the symbol of a shining dove, are libraries and centers of learning, reference and the arts, where the monks serve as librarians.
    • Training is long: from childhood a general education in culture and the arts, then advanced training in whichever field the student is best at and most interested in; choosing that field is a young Seeker's most important decision, since knowledge matters to them as much as physical perfection. Their style is Fist within Glove (see A Menagerie of Martial Arts), which suits their nonviolence. Initiates who show flaws in training are given posts in the monastery: teachers, librarians, scribes and other scholars.
    • A novice Seeker gains a minor sage ability: the player picks one sage special category (DMG p.32, such as humankind art, or demi-human laws and customs), and he is a sage with a minor field in that category only. His masters give him any special equipment it needs when he sets out.
    • Reasons to adventure: collecting. Sent to a region or country, he may serve a ruler as an indentured servant to pay for a needed piece, explore dangerous ruins for ancient treasures, or observe and record a people's customs. Buying art from greedy owners is expensive, so many Seekers also raise money by seeking donations, tutoring or adventuring.
    • (The article's scene: a Seeker travels alone to a barbarian lord's hall to offer gold for an ancient history book, and the lord can't believe anyone would risk his life for a book.)
  • The Brotherhood of the Black Lotus (lawful evil). Founded a few decades ago by a poor, lonely florist hungry for power and riches, who found the rare black lotus and learned its deadly use as a narcotic (see The Deadliest Perfume), and founded a temple devoted to growing it with a few monks who loved religion, power and beauty. As it prospered, brothers who wanted political power more than spiritual power did away with the founder, kept the black lotus as their symbol of beauty, grace and deadliness, and set out to control government through drugs, bribes and assassination, and to become the only religion in their land by destroying or discrediting every other monastic order.
    • Training is harsh: cruel, rigorous physical training and ego building, with arrogance and hatred of other orders drilled into initiates; kindness and mercy are punished severely, by death or expulsion. Their style is the cobra (see A Menagerie of Martial Arts), and they readily take swords and other deadly weapons as their weapon proficiencies. Every initiate is finally taught the herbalist skill, to handle and process the black lotus.
    • Reasons to adventure: bribery and assassination need huge sums, so many go adventuring to gather treasure for the masters; others are assigned to influential or wealthy characters to control them or draw them into the black lotus's embrace. The order works best as an enemy the characters must fight, or fall victim to.
    • (The article's scene: a lazy lord, kept on black lotus by a Brotherhood adviser, raises his people's taxes to make war on a rival order's temple, clearing the way for the Brotherhood.)
  • The Lawgivers (lawful neutral). A few monks survived when forest barbarians destroyed their temple, and decided the barbarians weren't bad or even evil, just undisciplined and uncivilized. Their mission is to bring every barbarian in their homeland to a civilized, lawful life by showing the benefits of civilization: kindness, force, intimidation, displays of prowess, whatever it takes. Their symbol is two crossed sticks inside a circle of chain: law and discipline within the endless cycle of life. Over the centuries they have had enough success with single tribes to stay hopeful, though the mission grows harder as the barbarians' own ways grow more complex. They care nothing whether a barbarian is good or evil, only that he accepts law and order.
    • They train to peak physical and mental perfection (to show that civilization makes tough warriors too, and to prepare for the confusion of a chaotic life), to endure hardship and discomfort, and to make their own decisions during long stays with tribes. Their style is escrima (see "Marshalling the Martial Arts," Dragon #122, and "Kicks and Sticks," #124), and a Lawgiver is never seen without his two escrima sticks (treat as jo sticks).
    • They can take nonweapon proficiencies from the barbarian list (OA Table 59) as well as the others. After their missions, many serve the barbarians as ambassadors, guides and counselors.
    • The order is fiercely vengeful against anyone who unjustly kills or injures a member; once a whole tribe of raiders was destroyed by a Lawgiver temple for sheltering a monk's killer, so that barbarian chiefs learn not to trifle with it.
    • Reasons to adventure: bodyguard, teacher or guide to a barbarian character; a long, hard mission set by a chief as a test or service, or just to get rid of him without angering his order; or tracking down and punishing someone who killed a fellow monk.
    • (The article's scene: a lone Lawgiver walks unarmed up to a band of desert raiders, deflects their thrown spears, knocks out five of them with his sticks, then bows to the khan and announces he has been sent to be his servant.)

With a little planning, light reading and imagination, monastic orders can make player characters, interesting neighbors or deadly foes. The article's sources: Donaldson, Lord Foul's Bane and The Illearth War (Del Rey, 1977); Shea, War of the Dragons (Jove, 1980) and Last of the Zinja (Jove, 1981); Shetterly, Witch Blood (Ace, 1986); Ward, Greyhawk Adventures (TSR, 1988).

Based on "Soldiers of the Law: When you need help, call for OA Law" by Dan Salas, Dragon #151 (November 1989), p.19-21. Samurai draw swords at the slightest insult, bushi and ronin pick fights to show their skill, kensai duels flare up and end in moments, and yakuza thugs threaten commoners at knife point. Without an alert, aggressive police force, a city would become a wasteland of burned buildings and bodies. Player characters may be used to tavern brawls and street duels going unpunished; this article adds the police who stop them.

Each territory's ruler keeps his own police within his borders, of one of two kinds: military police drawn from the regular army, or local police of commoners, mercenaries and a few soldiers. Either way, the army backs them in emergencies. All lawmen act as military police over commoners, travelers, strangers and the ruler's own warriors. They act swiftly against theft, assault, murder and dueling (which warlords see as a waste of manpower), and take their duty as seriously as a samurai takes loyalty to his lord. (The law courts above them are described on OA p.140.)

Ranks

  • Town commissioner: the chief of police of one town or city, often a 7th-9th level bushi, or in a major city or key town a 9th-12th level samurai. He supervises the police, reads reports of crime, decides which criminals are to be taken, and sometimes helps arrest a major criminal or a resisting official. A samurai commissioner always has at least 3d10 samurai under him, besides the bushi police.
  • Watchmen (patrolmen): the common police. Military police are samurai soldiers (1st-2nd level) and samurai officers (3rd-5th level). Local police are bushi warriors (1st-3rd level) with samurai or bushi officers; up to 25% of these bushi are commoners given the right to bear weapons, who become full warriors at 4th level.
  • Censors: secret agents: bushi-ninja, yakuza-ninja and genin. They rarely come from the ordinary ninja clans; the ruler's own leaders employ them to gather information for the police and to watch the police for corruption and conspiracy. Besides their ninja abilities, they can investigate as yakuza and interrogate prisoners.
  • Lowest police: zero-level bushi with 2-5 hit points each, given the worst jobs: guarding prisons, carrying out executions, and guarding those paraded in public as punishment. (In the article these are the eta, an outcast caste; OA Lite has no castes.)

Arms and armor

  • Fighting is a constant threat but rarely a daily event, so a soldier can't simply be moved from the battlefield to the street and called a policeman.
  • Only rich officers can afford full armor, worn only in the worst situations. On ordinary patrols lawmen wear padded armor and small metal helmets; officers expecting a fight wear chain mail, or more rarely full armor.
  • The lowest police carry only spears. Every other policeman has at least one sword, and those who aren't commoners wear the katana and wakizashi their warrior status allows.
  • Man catchers are clumsy to carry, so they are brought only when a particular criminal is sought.
  • Hooked spears can perform martial arts maneuvers: each lawman has 5% per level to know Weapon Catch, and if he does, 5% per level to know Weapon Breaker.
  • Sode garami entangle a loose sleeve or trouser leg: on a normal hit, the victim fights at -4 to hit and -2 damage. The penalties add up if he is caught by more than one.
  • Every officer carries a jitte as a mark of rank; it can perform Weapon Catch and Weapon Breaker. Officers often favor their own weapons, such as a chain weapon, lasso or whip, all meant to entangle without harm.
  • Preferring live prisoners, many police are skilled unarmed, especially in jujutsu: each lawman has 20% per level to know a martial art, with one special maneuver per two levels.

Making arrests

Lawmen first try to capture offenders for the courts, demanding peaceful surrender. If refused, they try to disarm, entangle or subdue them. A non-player samurai, kensai or ninja who is subdued usually tries to kill himself (seppuku, leaping from a ledge or cliff, or any other fatal act): 5% per level (the article adds the character's honor score, which OA Lite doesn't use). He must be physically restrained or he succeeds. This never applies to player characters, who act as they like. Only as a last resort do police use deadly force with edged weapons, and rarely long bows against dangerous criminals. Faced with overwhelming odds, the commissioner can ask the local lord for soldiers, and is rarely refused.

Police, yakuza and the town

Police and yakuza have an uneasy relationship. Where they are equal, the best they manage is suspicious tolerance. Where the yakuza are stronger, the police look tough but are timid with the gangs. Where the police are stronger, they are strict with commoners and brutal with criminals, hitting the gangs hard at every chance.

How many protectors (police or yakuza) a town has changes its encounters. Where there are few, crime and violence are everyday problems: people are suspicious and quick to defend themselves violently, commoners fear bullies and short-tempered warriors, and goods for sale are few and poor, since merchants won't risk their necks; the few who do keep bodyguards of bushi and ronin. In well-protected towns commoners thrive, rich merchants bring the best goods, craftsmen and farmers sell without fear, and only the most violent or foolish warriors fight without good reason.

Sample encounters

Only the first two should be used often.

  • The gate watch: 2-5 watchmen at every main city gate (fewer in small towns) watch everyone passing. Customs differ from land to land: in some the guards act only against wanted criminals or trouble; in some, important people such as officials and samurai (not clergy or peasants) must show written passes approved by the local lord at main gates and sometimes district gates (especially a castle district); in others the guards question anyone who looks suspicious (heavily armed foreigners, drawn swords or nocked arrows, open displays of magic), making reaction checks until they reach hostile (no entry) or friendly (let through). Where guards take bribes, it is typically 5 sp per watchman and 1 gp per officer (one and two tael), doubled if they have already turned hostile; elsewhere a bribe is an insult.
  • Wandering patrols: 2-5 watchmen; each turn there is a 25% chance one comes down a given street (check twice a turn if there is open fighting in the street or within earshot). Unless the fight is an approved vendetta duel, they order it stopped, and if disobeyed they fight to capture the offenders.
  • Prison: each city or large town has a one-room prison, usually at the city's edge, guarded by 5-20 of the lowest police and half as many bushi under a bushi officer, holding 20-80 people depending on the town's size and how the land is ruled (a corrupt land has more prisoners; one where police may kill freely, fewer).
  • Mistaken identity: watchmen surround the characters, weapons held ready but not attacking. In a few rounds an officer arrives, declares they aren't the criminals he wants, apologizes and leaves with his men. If the characters push for a fight, the police take them for guilty and try to capture them.
  • Public execution: peasants crowd round a wooden platform where at least one officer and six patrolmen oversee the executions, carried out by the lowest police. Thieves, murderers, pirates and other villains are boiled in oil; yakuza are swiftly beheaded. The characters may recognize a condemned man as a friend, an acquaintance or a source they need; a rescue may be in order.
  • The trapped fugitive: a dozen police and half a dozen soldiers surround a building (an inn, teahouse, merchant's compound) holding a dangerous fugitive, perhaps a high-level kensai, monk, samurai or wu jen, perhaps with a hostage. The police won't ask for help but will accept it for a reasonable price. If no one helps, they storm the building and kill the fugitive, losing half their men.
  • Collective responsibility: a desperate criminal (an unlucky commoner, a low-level yakuza, a treacherous ninja, a pretty girl) bursts into the characters' room and begs for help, offering a valuable reward if he can. The police soon arrive to search the rooms; characters caught hiding the criminal become outlaws themselves.
  • The informer: if the characters turn to crime, the police stay one step ahead, appearing at the worst times. Someone is spying on them: a beggar, a shopkeeper, one of the yakuza they deal with, or a censor watching from the rooftops in disguise.
  • Strike force: while the characters deal with local yakuza, a police strike force arrives to capture (or kill) a high-ranking yakuza leader, fighting only those who get in the way: 5-20 watchmen and one or two officers in as much armor as they have, and rarely 10-20 soldiers for a boss or underboss.
  • War in the streets: police and yakuza clash ever more violently, and rumor says the censors and yakuza killers are waging a war of assassinations, perhaps over an executed underboss or a beating given to the commissioner's brother. The city is full of terror and commoners are caught in the middle. The gangs are doomed, since heavily armed troops will come to restore order; many yakuza are already leaving, though most will fight to the end or go into hiding for years. The characters might join either side, or end up in trouble with both.

Player characters as police

Characters can join a police force or found one where there is none. A 9th-level samurai might be offered the post of town commissioner: about as powerful as the stewardship offered at 7th level, but as respected as a constable's post, since a commissioner often faces drawn swords where a constable rarely draws his. Local governments usually pay policemen 2 gp per level a month (four tael), officers twice that and commissioners three times. Experience comes from encounters with thugs, troublemakers, yakuza gangs, ninja clans and common criminals; the characters can declare war to clean up the town, or seek an uneasy peace with the gangs.
